planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade, ideally where its lax, trailing stems can spill over a wall or be trained on a support.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; trailing abutilon has a naturally lax, arching to trailing habit and small, maple-shaped leaves, with distinctive pendant, lantern-like flowers combining a swollen red calyx and bright yellow petals that hang like tiny paper lanterns nearly year-round in mild climates. Its trailing growth makes it well suited to hanging baskets, cascading over a low wall, or loosely trained against a trellis or fence, where the flowers are best appreciated from below. Hummingbirds visit the tubular blooms regularly, and the plant flowers most heavily with consistent moisture and light monthly feeding through the growing season. In zone 8, expect frost dieback most winters, with the plant often resprouting from the base if roots are protected by mulch; where hard freezes are common, grow it in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese lantern abutilon grows into a tall, upright shrub and benefits from occasional pinching to stay bushy rather than leggy.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese lantern abutilon grows into a tall, upright, somewhat leggy shrub with maple-like leaves and pendant, bell-shaped flowers in orange with distinctive dark red veining, the coloring that earned it the nickname candy corn plant among collectors. It blooms over a long season, often nearly year-round in essentially frost-free gardens, and is a reliable, easy-care source of hummingbird nectar with minimal pest or disease trouble. Pinch young plants regularly to encourage branching, since unpinched stems tend to grow tall and sparse rather than full and floriferous. Where winters bring hard freezes, expect significant dieback, with recovery from the roots likely if mulched; alternatively, grow it in a large container that can be moved to a sheltered spot for winter protection.

planting.note: Plant nursery starts after last frost into well-drained, average, fertile soil in full sun; grape-leaf flowering maple is a fast-growing Chilean shrub that prefers a Mediterranean-type climate with moderate humidity over intense heat and humidity.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average, fertile soil in full sun; grape-leaf flowering maple is a fast, large-growing Chilean shrub with soft, gray-green, grape-like leaves and an abundant spring display of large, saucer-shaped, mallow-like flowers in shades of lavender, blue-violet, or white, among the showiest blooms of any commonly grown abutilon. It grows quickly, often reaching full size within just a few years, making it useful for a fast privacy screen or a dramatic single-season specimen in mild-winter gardens. It performs best in climates with moderate summer humidity similar to its native Chilean range and can suffer more from prolonged intense heat and humidity than some of the more tropical abutilon species, so afternoon shade is worthwhile in the hottest, most humid parts of its zone range. Prune after flowering to control size and shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and protect the root zone with mulch through winter at the cooler edge of its hardiness.

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sea Island cotton needs an especially long, warm, humid growing season to produce its signature extra-long fiber.

directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm; Sea Island cotton is the extra-long-staple cotton species historically grown along the coastal Sea Islands of Georgia and South Carolina and now the source of premium Pima and Egyptian cotton fiber, distinct from the shorter-staple upland cotton grown across most of the Cotton Belt. Pale yellow, hibiscus-like flowers fade to pink before dropping, revealing bolls that mature more slowly than upland cotton and split open to reveal exceptionally long, silky, fine fibers prized by hand-spinners for their smooth, lustrous quality. It requires a longer, warmer, more humid growing season than upland cotton to fully mature its bolls, making it best suited to the Gulf Coast and Deep South rather than shorter-season northern climates. Watch for the same boll weevil and aphid pressures common to cotton generally, and rotate planting location yearly to limit soil-borne disease buildup.
